16.1.l: Arthroplasty — Knee Problems — Patella, Baja & Stiffness
16.1.t: Definition and Clinical Presentation of Patellar Maltracking
16.1.b:
The patella is the knee's commonest troublemaker after TKA, so we start by naming the problem.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is patellar maltracking after TKA?"
- "The patella runs **off-centre** in the trochlear groove, resurfaced or not."
- "It is the **commonest** TKA complication, and the cause is usually **component position**."
- "Merchant view for tilt or subluxation, then **CT for component rotation**."

### Definition and Significance
Maltracking is a position problem first, and a pain problem second.

#### Definition
- The patella sits off-centre in the groove, in flexion or extension
- It happens with or without **patellar resurfacing**
- It is the commonest TKA (total knee arthroplasty) complication, and the most **overlooked**
- It is also the commonest cause of a **poor outcome** after TKA

#### Consequences
- It brings **anterior knee pain**, subluxation or frank dislocation
- It also brings more wear and a higher fracture risk
- So the key answer is almost always **component position**, rarely the patella itself

### Clinical Presentation
The patient tells you the story, and the skyline film confirms it.

#### Clinical Assessment
- The patient has apprehension and anterior knee **pain on stairs**
- The **Merchant** (skyline) view shows lateral **tilt** or **subluxation** of the button
[[FIG: Fig 16.1 · 16.1
- Before surgery, the skyline view shows patellar dysplasia or trochlear hypoplasia
- Seeing them early lets you plan against maltracking

#### Computed Tomography for Unexplained Maltracking
- Unexplained maltracking → **CT for component rotation** before any soft-tissue surgery (Miller)
- Femoral rotation is read against the surgical TEA (transepicondylar axis), by **Berger**
- How rotation is measured → 10 TKA radiographs

### Intraoperative Assessment of Tracking
The best time to catch maltracking is before the wound is closed.

#### Set-Up
- Put the trials and a provisional spacer in, and leave the **retinaculum open**
- Ask one question: does the patella stay in the groove on its own?
- Adequate tracking means a **congruent** button, with little or no lateral pressure

#### No-Thumb Test
- Extend the knee, press the patella down from the suprapatellar pouch, then flex
- If the **medial facet lifts off** the medial condyle, the patella maltracks

#### The Hand-Held Patella
- A hand on the patella is **cheating**: it hides maltracking
- Take the hand off, and the patella dislocates

MEMORY HOOK — no thumbs, no cheating
- The no-thumb test is a closed-book exam: a thumb on the patella is a hidden cheat sheet.

#### Towel Clip Test and Full Flexion
- The **towel clip test** closes the open retinaculum with a clip while the knee moves
- If the patella tracks only when held, the test has failed
- Some surgeons test with no aid at all; very tight knees then tend to sublux
- Closure can hide maltracking, so test through **full flexion**: early tracking may fail deep

#### The Borderline Patella
- Put a **single stitch** at the superior pole, then check again
[[FIG: Fig 16.2 · 16.1

PITFALL — testing with the tourniquet up
- The tourniquet **tethers the quadriceps**, so the no-thumb test pulls falsely lateral (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- Say → "**deflate and re-test before any lateral release**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **No thumb · no closure · full flexion · tourniquet down**

16.2.l: Arthroplasty — Knee Problems — Patella, Baja & Stiffness
16.2.t: Pathomechanics: Q Angle, Patient and Implant Factors
16.2.b:
Now the why: almost every cause works by pulling the patella lateral, and the Q angle measures that pull.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is the Q angle and why does it matter?"
- "ASIS to patella centre, against patella centre to **tibial tuberosity**."
- "A bigger angle means a bigger **lateral pull**, so the patella subluxes laterally."
- "Anything that **raises the Q angle** causes maltracking, so restoring it is a TKA goal."

### Q Angle
The Q angle is the line of the quadriceps pull compared with the line of the patellar tendon.

#### Definition
- One line runs from the ASIS (anterior superior iliac spine) to the patella centre
- The other runs from the patella centre to the **tibial tuberosity**
[[FIG: Fig 16.3 · 16.2
- Campbell (after Hvid) uses the extended **femoral anatomic axis** for the first line

#### Measurement
- Measure it with the knee extended and the quadriceps relaxed
- It falls in flexion, as the patella seats in the groove

PITFALL — which normal Q angle?
- Handbook 10–15° (men 10–13°, women 12–15°); Prof Abdel Karim 13–18°, women ≈18°
- Say → "**about 15°, women higher** (wider pelvis); abnormal >15° in men, >20° in women (Campbell)"

### Medial Patellar Restraints
Against the lateral pull stand two restraints, one moving and one fixed.
- The quadriceps pulls along the femoral axis, except the **VMO** (vastus medialis obliquus)
- The VMO medialises the patella in extension: it is the **dynamic** restraint
- The **MPFL** (medial patellofemoral ligament) is the **static** restraint to lateral shift

### Q Angle and Lateral Subluxation
A larger angle tips the balance towards the lateral side.
- A larger Q angle gives more **lateral subluxation** force
[[FIG: Fig 16.4 · 16.2
- Past a tolerable limit, the lateral pull and **shear** on the patella cause maltracking
- A lateral tubercle or a medial trochlea enlarges that lateral vector
- So restoring the Q angle is a TKA goal, even without resurfacing

MEMORY HOOK — the bowstring
- The quadriceps is a bowstring: the bigger the Q angle, the harder it flicks the patella lateral.

The causes fall into three groups: the **patient**, the **implant design** and the **surgical technique**.
The first two come here; technique has its own part (16.3).

### Patient Factors
Some knees arrive with less margin for error.

#### Previous Knee Pathology
- Neglected **PF (patellofemoral) arthritis** or old instability is not causal alone, but leaves less margin
- **Trochlear dysplasia** and a previous dislocation predict instability after TKA
- Instability factors may show only after TKA, never before it

#### Genu Valgum
- **Residual genu valgum** raises the Q angle
[[FIG: Fig 16.5 · 16.2
- Valgus **>20°** often comes with subluxation (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Valgus, femoral anteversion and external tibial torsion all push the patella into valgus
- So correct the valgus fully at TKA

#### Lateral Release in Valgus Knees
- A valgus knee has a lateral tubercle and a tight lateral retinaculum
- So it needs a **lateral release** more often

#### Patella Alta
- The patella first touches the trochlea at ≈**20°** of flexion (Campbell)
- The Handbook puts entry at **20–30°**; alta delays it beyond **40°** (Handbook)
- From 0–20°, the **MPFL and VMO** hold it; from 30°, the trochlea centres it
- **Patella alta** enters the groove late, so the unprotected range is longer and it is unstable

### Implant Design
Design can help the patella, but it cannot undo a surgeon's error.

#### Patella-Friendly and Patella-Unfriendly Femoral Components
- Older **patella-unfriendly** designs, with a short anterior flange, had more patellar problems
- **Patella-friendly** designs have a longer flange, running further distally
- Their lateral flange is higher, because maltracking goes lateral
- They also keep a continuous anterior **radius of curvature**

#### Benefits of Patella-Friendly Design
- It captures the patella earlier in flexion
- Its raised lateral wall acts as the native buttress
- A built-in **trochlear groove angle** of up to **7°** improves tracking
[[FIG: Fig 16.6 · 16.2

#### Limits of Design
- Trochlea, femoral rotation, patellar thickness and joint line together mean fewer **lateral releases**
- Resurfacing choices → 16.3 Patellar resurfacing

#### Patellar Button Shape
- **Dome** buttons tolerate rotational mismatch, but anatomic buttons need exact orientation
- But no design **can rescue** an internally rotated component

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Valgus · alta · dysplasia · friendly flange · 7° groove · rotation beats design**

16.3.l: Arthroplasty — Knee Problems — Patella, Baja & Stiffness
16.3.t: Surgical Technique: Component Position and Patellar Preparation
16.3.b:
Component position is the commonest cause, and every error here works the same way: it raises the Q angle.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "which surgical errors cause maltracking?"
- "**Femur or tibia internally rotated or medialised**: the patella ends up relatively lateral."
- "**Patellar button lateral**: the Q angle rises; the button always goes medial."
- "Rule: **lateralise everything except the patella**."

### Femoral Component
The femur carries the groove, so where the femur goes, the groove goes.

#### Rotation
- **Internal rotation** (IR) moves the trochlea medially
[[FIG: Fig 16.7 · 16.3
- So the patella **subluxes laterally**; aim for slight ER instead
[[FIG: Fig 16.8 · 16.3
- Cut parallel to the TEA, perpendicular to Whiteside's line, or 3° ER to the posterior condyles
- Flexion-gap shape, femoral rotation and the hypoplastic condyle → 08 Technique

#### Mediolateral Position
- A **medialised** femur puts the trochlea medial to the tubercle, so the Q angle rises
- Keep it **central**, with its centre a few millimetres lateral to the notch centre
- Between sizes, **lateralise** and cover the lateral condyle

#### Size
- An **oversized** femur puts the trochlea too anterior: instability or limited flexion
- Oversizing also brings **overhang pain**, the commonest size problem
- It tightens the gaps and raises PF force and shear, so the patella maltracks

#### Flexion and Extension
- A **flexed** femur lifts the flange, so the descending patella impinges on its edge
- An **extended** femur overstuffs the joint: anterior pain and less flexion

### Tibial Component
The tibia carries the tubercle, so its errors move the tubercle instead.

#### Rotation
- A tray in IR means relative **ER of the tubercle**
[[FIG: Fig 16.9 · 16.3
- The femoral component rotates with the tray, but the tubercle stays behind
- So the tubercle sits lateral, and the Q angle rises
- Tray IR also brings unexplained **pain and stiffness**

#### Mediolateral Position
- A **medialised** tray puts the joint medial to the tubercle, so the Q angle rises
- Femoral and tibial IR together give maltracking, more pain and worse complications

#### Rotational Landmarks and Overhang
- Rotation is **central or external**, never internal
- Lateralise the tray on the lateral cortex
- Centre it over the **medial third** of the tubercle (Miller); other landmarks → 08 Technique
[[FIG: Fig 16.10 · 16.3
- A tray **overhanging medially** irritates the medial ligament: pain and altered tracking
- Excess external rotation does the same

PITFALL — the Handbook's direction error
- The Handbook prints femoral or tibial IR as "patella medial": the wrong direction
- Say → "**IR of either component sends the patella lateral**, so the Q angle rises"

### Patellar Resurfacing
Whether to resurface is the oldest patellar debate; the evidence is mixed.

#### Arguments and Evidence
- Resurfacing gives less **anterior knee pain** and better PF function
- Opponents quote complications of 5–60%; Prof Sherif Khaled's own are 5–10%
- PF complications: **4%** resurfaced vs **12%** unresurfaced (Campbell)
- Anterior knee pain at 5 years: **25%** unresurfaced vs **5%** resurfaced
- Secondary resurfacing relieves less pain, with more fracture and stiffness

#### Indications
- **Mandatory**: very advanced PF arthritis, and inflammatory disease (RA, SLE, ankylosing spondylitis)
- Leave it in OA with good cartilage, no eburnation and congruent tracking
- Also needed for leaving it: normal patellar shape, no crystal or inflammatory arthropathy
- Lighter patients do well with a native patella

#### Selective Resurfacing
- A native patella in an anatomic groove scores as well as a resurfaced one
- But the Australian registry found **higher revision** with selective than routine resurfacing (Campbell)
- PS knees with unresurfaced patellae also had more revisions
- CR knees with resurfaced patellae had the fewest; **onlay** buttons beat inlay
- Most Egyptian surgeons do not resurface; Prof Shokry never has

#### Technique
- A sizer or caliper measures the patella; a clamp holds it for a level cut
- Drill three peg holes with a **stopper** drill bit; no stopper → perforation and fracture
[[FIG: Fig 16.11 · 16.3
- Cement the button and keep the clamp closed until the cement sets

#### Patelloplasty
- Without a button, do a full **patelloplasty**: remove osteophytes and file the surface
- Add lateral facetectomy, drill sclerotic bone, and excise excess fat pad and synovium
- Circumferential diathermy **denervates** the patella: less anterior knee pain
- Diathermy "circumcision" alone is not enough

### Patellar Component
The patella is the one component that goes medial, and its cut matters as much as its place.

#### Mediolateral Position
- The button always goes **medial**: medial lowers the Q angle, lateral raises it
[[FIG: Fig 16.12 · 16.3
- It counters the valgus force, as the only component placed medially
- The patellar ridge lies **medial**, not central; the button sits over the thicker bone
[[FIG: Fig 16.13 · 16.3

#### Degree of Medialisation
- Medialise it to the **median eminence**, not the centre of the bone
- The right position is ≈**2–3 mm** medialised (Handbook)

#### Consequences of Malposition
- A centralised button forces the patella to track with a **higher Q angle**
- A lateral button loses the median eminence, so it subluxes laterally in extension
- A medial button leaves lateral bone bare, which impinges → **lateral facetectomy**

#### Patellar Resection
- A symmetric posterior cut on asymmetric facets gives **tilt**
[[FIG: Fig 16.14 · 16.3
- So cut the facets to equal thickness, and the button sits flat
- The **lateral facet** cut is often much shallower than the medial
- Cut medially below the articular surface, laterally at its level
- Plan what you **leave**: 25 mm patella − 9 mm = 16 mm left (Handbook)

#### Thickness
- Total thickness after resurfacing is **20–23 mm**; buttons are **8.5–10 mm** (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- Leave at least **12–13 mm** of bone; some books say up to 16 mm
- A patella under 12–13 mm cannot be resurfaced
- Too thin → fracture during cementing or through the peg holes
- Restore the patella's **thickness**, so the joint is not overstuffed
- Patellar clamp and caliper → 07 Knee design

#### Vertical Position and Overhang
- A **superior** button acts like alta, with delayed entry into the groove
- An **inferior** button acts like baja: overstuffing and less flexion
- Height is central, may be superior, but **never inferior**
- A button overhanging proximally is one cause of the **patellar clunk syndrome**
[[FIG: Fig 16.15 · 16.3

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Medial · slightly superior · equal facets · same thickness**

### Joint Line
The joint line sets patellar height, so moving it changes the patella too.

- A **raised** joint line gives a relative **baja**; a **lowered** one a relative **alta**
- Raised **>8 mm**: less motion, PF pain, maltracking, instability, even fractures (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- Causes, the **4 mm** limit and the joint-line rules → 08 Technique; true vs apparent baja → 16.5

### Lateralisation Rule
Four errors send the patella lateral, and one rule prevents them all.

| Component | Error that sends the patella lateral |
|---|---|
| Femoral | **internal rotation** · **medialised** · flexed or extended |
| Tibial | **internal rotation** · medialised |
| Patellar | **lateralised** · wrong resection |
| Joint line | tibial cut, **distal femoral** cut, insert thickness |

- The four errors push the patella lateral, then the Q angle rises
[[FIG: Fig 16.16 · 16.3
- So **lateralise anything except the patella**; rotation and side-to-side position are the keys
- Soft-tissue surgery alone treats the symptom, so find the malpositioned component
- Any malalignment also risks PF instability, patellar fracture and **stiffness**

MEMORY HOOK — everyone out but the patella
- At the knee party everyone shuffles lateral; only the patella takes the medial seat.

- The patellar ridge lies **medial**, not central; the button sits over the thicker bone
[[FIG: Fig 16.13 · 16.3

#### Degree of Medialisation
- Medialise it to the **median eminence**, not the centre of the bone
- The right position is ≈**2–3 mm** medialised (Handbook)

#### Consequences of Malposition
- A centralised button forces the patella to track with a **higher Q angle**
- A lateral button loses the median eminence, so it subluxes laterally in extension
- A medial button leaves lateral bone bare, which impinges → **lateral facetectomy**

#### Patellar Resection
- A symmetric posterior cut on asymmetric facets gives **tilt**
[[FIG: Fig 16.14 · 16.3
- So cut the facets to equal thickness, and the button sits flat
- The **lateral facet** cut is often much shallower than the medial
- Cut medially below the articular surface, laterally at its level
- Plan what you **leave**: 25 mm patella − 9 mm = 16 mm left (Handbook)

#### Thickness
- Total thickness after resurfacing is **20–23 mm**; buttons are **8.5–10 mm** (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- Leave at least **12–13 mm** of bone; some books say up to 16 mm
- A patella under 12–13 mm cannot be resurfaced
- Too thin → fracture during cementing or through the peg holes
- Restore the patella's **thickness**, so the joint is not overstuffed
- Patellar clamp and caliper → 07 Knee design

#### Vertical Position and Overhang
- A **superior** button acts like alta, with delayed entry into the groove
- An **inferior** button acts like baja: overstuffing and less flexion
- Height is central, may be superior, but **never inferior**
- A button overhanging proximally is one cause of the **patellar clunk syndrome**
[[FIG: Fig 16.15 · 16.3

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Medial · slightly superior · equal facets · same thickness**

16.3.5.l: Arthroplasty — Knee Problems — Patella, Baja & Stiffness
16.3.5.b:
The joint line sets patellar height, so moving it changes the patella too.

- A **raised** joint line gives a relative **baja**; a **lowered** one a relative **alta**
- Raised **>8 mm**: less motion, PF pain, maltracking, instability, even fractures (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- Causes, the **4 mm** limit and the joint-line rules → 08 Technique; true vs apparent baja → 16.5

16.3.6.l: Arthroplasty — Knee Problems — Patella, Baja & Stiffness
16.3.6.b:
Four errors send the patella lateral, and one rule prevents them all.

| Component | Error that sends the patella lateral |
|---|---|
| Femoral | **internal rotation** · **medialised** · flexed or extended |
| Tibial | **internal rotation** · medialised |
| Patellar | **lateralised** · wrong resection |
| Joint line | tibial cut, **distal femoral** cut, insert thickness |

- The four errors push the patella lateral, then the Q angle rises
[[FIG: Fig 16.16 · 16.3
- So **lateralise anything except the patella**; rotation and side-to-side position are the keys
- Soft-tissue surgery alone treats the symptom, so find the malpositioned component
- Any malalignment also risks PF instability, patellar fracture and **stiffness**

MEMORY HOOK — everyone out but the patella
- At the knee party everyone shuffles lateral; only the patella takes the medial seat.

16.4.l: Arthroplasty — Knee Problems — Patella, Baja & Stiffness
16.4.b:
With the cause known, treatment climbs a ladder from the cheapest step to revision.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you manage maltracking?"
- "On the table: **deflate the tourniquet**, then partial, then complete **lateral release**."
- "Then resurface, then **reposition the malpositioned component**; never release over malrotation."
- "Late: physiotherapy, CT, then **revise the component**; tubercle osteotomy only with great caution."

### Intraoperative Management
Each step is tried only when the one before has failed.
- **Tourniquet deflation** comes first: the cheapest step, a false problem before a real one
- Deflation spared a release in **31%**; in another study **48%** reverted to normal (Campbell)

| Step after deflation | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | Partial lateral release |
| 2 | Complete lateral release |
| 3 | Patellar resurfacing, even without prior PF arthritis |
| 4 | Reposition the malpositioned component |

MEMORY HOOK — let the air out first
- Let the air out before you get the knife out: deflation alone spared a release in **31%**.

### Lateral Retinacular Release
A release frees a tight lateral side, but it costs blood supply.

#### Technique
- Poor tracking only in flexion → a standard **lateral release**; muscle is not cut (Prof Shokry)
- Start with **pie-crusting**; if the patella responds, stop there
- If not, extend the incision and leave it unsutured
- The cut runs from **Gerdy tubercle** to the vastus lateralis fibres; small bands often suffice

#### Protection of the Patellar Blood Supply
- It is commonly done from inside the joint
- Release from outside exposes the **superior lateral genicular artery** at the vastus lateralis junction
[[FIG: Fig 16.17 · 16.4
- So the artery can be spared; the risk is patellar **AVN** (avascular necrosis) and fracture (Campbell)
- The risk is worse after a medial parapatellar arthrotomy

#### Complications
- Release brings more pain, swelling, slower rehabilitation and wound problems
- Still, these cost less than a subluxing patella

Patellar fracture after TKA → 15 Periprosthetic fractures.

### Late Maltracking
A late problem gets the same logic: rehabilitate, image, then fix the cause.

#### Conservative Treatment
- Begin with strengthening and physiotherapy
- If that fails, re-explore, with or without the button

#### Surgical Treatment
- Components well placed: release, rarely enough alone, then **proximal realignment**
- Malposition: inspect and **revise** the component; release over malrotation fails
- A button placed **medially and superiorly** solves dislocation or rotation problems
- A ruptured medial capsular repair lets the patella drift lateral
- Close the capsule at **90°** of flexion, then check tracking through full motion (Campbell)

#### Distal Realignment
- **Distal realignment** (tibial tubercle osteotomy) needs extreme caution
- Its nonunion is a serious loss

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Deflate · release · resurface · reposition · revise**

### Other Patellofemoral Complications
Not every patellar complaint is maltracking: the clunk, the click and the loose button.

#### Patellar Clunk Syndrome
- A fibrous nodule forms on the quadriceps tendon, just above the superior pole
- It catches in the PS box and "clunks" at **30–45°** on active extension (Campbell)
- Causes: a proximally overhanging button, or an early PS design with a sharp sulcus
- Treat by arthroscopic debridement; open excision if it recurs
- Prevent it by limited synovectomy behind the quadriceps tendon in PS knees

#### Click and Component Failure
- A **click** is often the patella on the anterior flange, more with mobile bearings
- Patellar component loosening occurs in **0.6–2.4%** (Campbell)
- Metal-backed buttons fail by wear, delamination and peg fracture: revise early

16.5.l: Arthroplasty — Knee Problems — Patella, Baja & Stiffness
16.5.b:
From a patella that drifts sideways we move to one that sits too low.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is patella baja after TKA and how do you treat it?"
- "A low patella **relative to the joint line** hits the insert in flexion: pain, maltracking."
- "**Truly short tendon** (scar, old surgery) or **apparent baja** (raised joint line, low button)."
- "Release, lower the joint line, **proximalise the tubercle**; patellectomy last."

### Definition and Assessment
Height is judged against the joint line, because that is where the patella meets the implant.

#### Definition
- Judge height against the **joint line**, not the tubercle
[[FIG: Fig 16.18 · 16.5
- After TKA it comes from **tendon contracture** plus a joint line raised above the tubercle

#### Clinical Effects
- A low patella strikes the **tibial insert** in flexion
[[FIG: Fig 16.19 · 16.5
- So the patient has anterior pain and less flexion

#### Measurement
- Insall–Salvati <0.8 means baja
- The **modified Insall–Salvati** ratio measures only the articular part, and is replacing it
- After TKA, **Blackburne–Peel** and joint-line landmarks are used → 10 TKA radiographs

MEMORY HOOK — the doorstop
- A low patella is a doorstop: as the knee bends, it jams against the insert.

### Aetiology
Some baja is born, some is scarred, and some is made at the TKA itself.

#### True Patellar Tendon Shortening
- It may be **congenital**
- More often it is scar after an **opening-wedge HTO** (high tibial osteotomy)
- Or after **tubercle distalisation** or a **tendon repair**

So a truly short tendon is hard to fix.

#### Scarring after Osteotomy
- Immobilisation, new bone at the insertion and fibrosis shorten the tendon
- Early quadriceps work prevents it
- HTO also changes slope and tubercle, so TKA exposure is harder

#### Apparent Baja
- Apparent baja is avoidable at TKA
- It comes from an **inferior patellar button**
- Or from an **excess distal femoral cut**, which raises the joint line

#### Tendon Repair
- In a quadriceps tendon repair, watch the patella's sagittal position to avoid alta or baja

### Management
The ladder goes from releasing the tissue to moving the bone.

#### Release and Lowering the Joint Line
- Step 1: release the tight structures at surgery
- Step 2: **lower the joint line**, with more tibial cut and a **distal femoral augment** (Miller)
[[FIG: Fig 16.20 · 16.5

#### Tibial Tubercle Proximalisation
- **Tubercle proximalisation** is best for a stiff TKA under 90° of flexion with baja
- Native post-traumatic stiffness, Caton index **<0.4**: tubercle proximalisation plus open arthrolysis (Campbell)
- Baja found at revision → move the fragment **proximally** and excise the proximal bone
- Otherwise the fragment leaves a bony prominence in front of the knee

#### Tibial Tubercle Osteotomy Technique
- Its length, cut, closure and pictures → 08 TKA technique (Extensile Approaches)

#### Patellectomy
- **Patellectomy** is the salvage
- It shortens the quadriceps lever arm, so extension is weaker

PITFALL — the tibial cut alone
- More tibial cut alone opens both gaps; the line falls only with femoral augments
- Say → "**more tibial cut plus distal femoral augments lowers the joint line**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Judge vs joint line · short tendon vs raised line · release, lower line, tubercle up, patellectomy last**

16.6.l: Arthroplasty — Knee Problems — Patella, Baja & Stiffness
16.6.b:
A low patella is one cause of a stiff knee; now the stiff knee as a whole.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you approach a stiff TKA?"
- "First exclude **infection**, then split **mechanical** from **biological** causes."
- "Mechanical (tight gaps, overstuffing, baja) needs **revision**; scar alone needs lysis."
- "**MUA** (manipulation under anaesthesia) works early, at **4–12 weeks**."

### Definitions
Stiffness, flexion deformity and extension lag are different, and examiners ask the difference.

| Term | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Stiffness** | arc of motion lost, mainly flexion; stiff TKA = **<90° flexion** (Miller) |
| **Flexion deformity** | the knee cannot be **passively** extended; in a balanced TKA, tight hamstrings |
| **Extension lag** | passive extension full, **active** falls short: quadriceps weakness (Campbell) |

### Aetiology
Most causes are mechanical, and the last one is a diagnosis of exclusion.

| Group | Cause | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Tight gaps** | PCL · capsule or gastrocnemius | flexion gap · extension gap |
| **Closure** | tight retinacular closure | less flexion |
| **Patella baja** | low patella | limits flexion |
| **Overstuffed PF** | thick patella · femur in extension | prominent flange, pain |
| **Guarding** | hamstring spasm · infection | protective stiffness |

- A femur placed in extension lifts the anterior profile and overstuffs the PF joint (16.3)
- **Arthrofibrosis** is excess scar with no mechanical cause: a diagnosis of exclusion
- It caused **4.5%** of 781 TKA revisions (Campbell)

### Investigation
Infection hides behind stiffness, so it is ruled out first.
- Check CRP, ESR and aspirate → 11 Painful arthroplasty, 12 PJI
- Then decide: mechanical or biological

### Management
The fix matches the cause: bone and implants for a block, lysis for scar.

#### Treatment by Cause
- **Revision** for tight gaps or wrong components
- **Lysis**, arthroscopic or open, for scar only
- A preoperative flexion deformity needs posterior capsular release and posterior osteophyte removal

#### Manipulation under Anaesthesia
- **MUA** works between **4 and 12 weeks** after primary TKA (Miller)
- Late MUA risks periprosthetic fracture and extensor rupture (Campbell)
- Manipulation is a known cause of **patellar tendon rupture**
- Avoid it if the femur is notched

MEMORY HOOK — the MUA shop window
- MUA is a shop open from week **4** to week **12**: come later, leave with a fracture.

#### Exposure of the Stiff Knee
- A **quadriceps snip** opens a stiff or fibrosed knee, or a patella that will not evert
[[FIG: Fig 16.21 · 16.6
- It extends the arthrotomy obliquely upwards, parallel to the vastus lateralis fibres
- The **V-Y quadriceps turndown** is kept for revisions only

#### Prevention
- Close every TKA **in flexion**, so flexion is there from day one
- Walk with a walker from day one, with **no flexion restriction**
- Encourage extension with the foot on a pillow, and flexion by dangling the legs
- CPM is kept for extreme preoperative arthrofibrosis

#### Night Splint for Flexion Deformity
- A preoperative flexion deformity gets a **night splint** (Prof Shokry)
- Because body image returns the knee to flexion
- Or a pillow under the leg, not the knee
- Then 2 weeks free with a walker, then physiotherapy

PITFALL — manipulating a mechanical block
- MUA or lysis cannot fix a tight gap, an overstuffed joint or baja
- Say → "**infection out, films for components and gaps, then MUA only for scar**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Infection first · mechanical = revise · scar = lysis · MUA 4–12 weeks · splint the flexed knee at night**
